nameStory: The Japanese House Centipede gets its name from its origins in Japan (along with China and Korea) and its habit of living alongside humans in our homes and buildings. Unlike many centipedes that prefer the great outdoors, this species has mastered the art of indoor living, making our basements, closets, and bathrooms their preferred hunting grounds.
description: The Japanese House Centipede is a fast-moving predator with an unmistakable appearance - imagine a creature that looks like it's wearing extremely long, delicate leg warmers! This centipede has a flattened, segmented body that's typically yellowish-brown with darker stripes. What makes it truly distinctive are its incredibly long, thin legs that seem to float around its body as it moves with surprising speed and grace.

idTips.label: Ultra-long legs
idTips.description: The legs are almost ethereal-looking - much longer than the body itself and so thin they seem to shimmer as the centipede moves. They feel delicate but are surprisingly strong.

idTips.label: Flattened body shape
idTips.description: The body is noticeably flattened from top to bottom, unlike the more cylindrical shape of many other centipedes. It feels almost paper-thin if you were to gently touch it.

idTips.label: Yellowish-brown coloration
idTips.description: The body has a pale yellowish-brown base color with darker brown stripes running lengthwise. The coloration can appear almost translucent in bright light.

idTips.label: Lightning-fast movement
idTips.description: When disturbed, it moves with startling speed in a flowing, undulating motion that's quite different from the more rigid movement of other centipedes.

idTips.label: Indoor habitat preference
idTips.description: Unlike most centipedes, you'll typically find this species inside buildings rather than under logs or rocks outdoors.

habitat: Japanese House Centipedes are most commonly found inside human structures - basements, bathrooms, closets, and other areas with moderate moisture levels. They prefer spaces that stay relatively cool and humid, often hiding in cracks and crevices during the day. While they're occasionally found outdoors under building foundations or in crawl spaces, they're much more adapted to indoor living than most centipedes.

seasonality.spring: Active indoors year-round, but you might notice more activity in spring as they begin hunting for increased insect prey. Look for them in damp indoor spaces.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most likely to be spotted darting across floors or walls, especially in humid indoor areas like basements and bathrooms.
seasonality.fall: Remain active indoors as outdoor temperatures drop. This is when you're most likely to encounter them as they may be more visible while seeking shelter deeper in buildings.
seasonality.winter: Continue to be active in heated indoor spaces, making them one of the few centipedes you can observe year-round in New England homes.

funFact: Despite having the word 'centipede' in their name, Japanese House Centipedes actually have 15 pairs of legs (30 total), not 100 - and those incredibly long legs can regenerate if lost, growing back even longer than before!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the Common House Centipede (Scutigera coleoptrata), which is much more widespread in New England. The Japanese House Centipede is typically smaller and has a more yellowish coloration, while the Common House Centipede tends to be larger with more grayish tones and banded legs.
contextualKnowledge: This is a relatively recent arrival to North America, having been introduced from East Asia. With only 5 recorded observations in New England, it's still quite rare in our region compared to the much more common house centipede species that most people encounter indoors.
compareHints: Since this is the only Thereuonema species in New England, compare it to the Common House Centipede in the genus Scutigera. The Japanese House Centipede is generally smaller, more yellowish in color, and has a more delicate appearance overall. The Common House Centipede has more distinct banding on its legs and a more robust build.
